stops.name: Monte Verità, Sang an die Sonne: the sun sung down and up
stops.campa: At the close of the great congress on the mountain, Laban stages Sang an die Sonne across a whole night: the sun's descent danced at evening over the lake; at midnight, before Gusto Gräser's grotto, the demons of the night; at dawn the choir greets the rising sun as the promise that the war-winter of the world will end. Wigman dances on the meadow among the torches, priestess now, not pupil, in the movement choir consecrated as liturgy for a religion of the body, performed while the guns hold Europe.

stops.name: The Walensee, the sanatorium and the Seven Dances written in fever
stops.campa: The war years call in their debt: her stepfather dead, her brother home from the front with a limb gone, a love ended, the partnership with Laban strained past bearing. She breaks, and is carried to a sanatorium above the Walensee in eastern Switzerland. Half a year she lies between the cliff and the grey lake, and there, unable to dance, she writes dance: Die sieben Tänze des Lebens, a dance-poem of desire, sorrow, the demon and death, composed entire in a notebook by a woman who cannot stand. The work waits three years for a body.

stops.name: Berlin, the Philharmonie nearly empty
stops.campa: Risen from the sanatorium, thirty-two years old, she carries her strange gospel to Berlin and hires the Philharmonie. The hall is nearly empty; the capital, hungry and revolutionary, has no eyes yet for a woman dancing daemons without music. The failure is total and does not matter. She has seen what she is for, and an artist who has written dances from a sickbed is not to be refused by an empty room. She gathers the cycle, Ecstatic Dances, the temple pieces, and carries it from city to city like a contagion looking for its climate.

stops.name: Dresden, the hall of the merchants' guild says yes
stops.campa: On 7 November 1919, in the hall of the Dresden Kaufmannschaft, the climate is found. The city of the Brücke painters, primed by a decade of expressionism, recognizes at once what Berlin shrugged at: the evening is an extraordinary public triumph, and the merchants' guild-hall, of all rooms the temple of her father's class, is where the merchant's daughter is finally received as what she is. Dresden adopts her. Within a year she will plant her school here, and for two decades the city on the Elbe will be the Jerusalem of the absolute dance.

stops.name: Dresden, the school opens at the Postplatz
stops.campa: In 1920, with the devotion and the purse of her Swiss pupil Berthe Trümpy, she opens her own school in rooms of the Palasthotel Weber on the Postplatz. There is little money, less coal, and a doctrine: not steps but Gestaltung, the shaping of inner experience into visible form. Girls arrive from across the broken Reich and beyond it, hungry in every sense, and are put to the breath, the swing, the fall, the drum. The Wigman school will become the mother-house of an order that spreads to four cities and across an ocean.

stops.name: Dresden, the chamber dance group before the Philharmonic
stops.campa: On 14 January 1921 her first chamber dance group steps out with the Philharmonic in the Dresden concert hall; Wigman no longer a lone daimon but the center of a constellation: Berthe Trümpy, and soon the fierce young Gret Palucca, Yvonne Georgi, Hanya Holm, Harald Kreutzberg. Her credo is already law in the studio: ecstasy without form is convulsion, form without ecstasy is gymnastics; the dance is real only where the two are fused. The group tours, and Germany learns that the new dance is not one woman's seizure but a school, a language, an estate.
stops.quote: Without ecstasy no dance! Without form no dance!
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman's credo, in The Mary Wigman Book, ed. Walter Sorell (1975)

stops.name: Frankfurt, Die sieben Tänze des Lebens made flesh
stops.campa: On 14 December 1921, at the Frankfurt opera house, the notebook from the Walensee sanatorium at last finds its bodies: Die sieben Tänze des Lebens is danced whole: the dance of longing, of love, of lust, of sorrow, the demon's dance, the dance of death, and through the veil of the last dance, life. What was written by a woman who could not stand is performed by the school she raised in the meantime. The canon reads the premiere as a resurrection performed in public: the illness composed, the composition now breathing.

stops.name: Dresden, the house on the Bautzner Strasse
stops.campa: The school outgrows hotel rooms and settles into its true temple, the villa grounds at Bautzner Strasse 107 above the Elbe: studios, garden, gong and drum, the hill-house where a generation of the century's dancers is formed. Palucca departs to found her own school, as daughters of this house do; Georgi, Kreutzberg, Holm carry the doctrine outward. Here Wigman teaches that dance is no entertainment of the theatres but a language older than them, and the pupils learn to speak it from the breath outward. The house still stands; dancers still keep it.
stops.quote: The dance is a living language which speaks of man — an artistic message soaring above the ground of reality in order to speak, on a higher level, in images and allegories of man's innermost emotions and need for communication.
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (trans. Walter Sorell, 1966), opening

stops.name: Dresden, Hexentanz II: the witch returns wearing a face
stops.campa: In 1926 the witch of the Palais Porcia comes back, and this time she has a face: a carved mask, remote and terrible, made after Wigman's own features and estranged from them. To rattles and percussion she dances seated and clawed, hammering the floor, the body shapeless in brocade, the mask smiling its fixed smile. The canon tells how the dance was given to her: late one night, hair wild over her nightgown, she catches herself in the mirror, and the mirror shows her the other one. The minutes of film that survive are the icon of Ausdruckstanz itself.
stops.quote: The image of one possessed, wild and dissolute, repelling and fascinating... there she was — the witch — the earth-bound creature with her unrestrained, naked instincts.
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (trans. Walter Sorell, 1966), on Hexentanz

stops.name: Essen, the Second Dancers' Congress
stops.campa: At Essen the German dancers convene their second parliament, and the estate that Magdeburg founded now divides into its churches: Laban unveils his script, the kinetography that will bear his name; the ballet masters defend the theatres; and Wigman stands for the absolute dance: dance sovereign, serving neither opera nor notation nor decoration. The debates are doctrinal because the stakes are doctrinal: a new art is writing its constitution. She argues, as always, from the body outward, suspicious of every system that would fix in signs what lives only in the breath.

stops.name: Dresden, Schwingende Landschaft: the swinging landscape
stops.campa: At the Dresden Schauspielhaus she dances the solo cycle Schwingende Landschaft, the swinging landscape, seven dances in which the daimon rests and the earth itself moves through her: summer's pastorale, the seraphic song, the wind's turning. After the witches and death-dances of the decade the canon reads this cycle as her psalter, the gentlest page in her book. She is at the summit: schools in Dresden, Berlin, Hamburg, Erfurt, Frankfurt; London conquered the year before; and across the water an impresario named Hurok is already counting the houses she will fill.

stops.name: Munich, Totenmal: the call to the dead of the war
stops.campa: At the Third Dancers' Congress in Munich, in a vast hall raised on the Theresienwiese, she and the poet Albert Talhoff stage Totenmal on 24 June 1930: a monument in word, light and movement to the dead of the Great War, speaking choirs against choirs of dancers, the women calling and the fallen answering, Wigman herself moving between the living and the dead as the veiled figure at the threshold. Sixteen hundred watch at each performance. The canon keeps Totenmal as the high mass of the movement choir, and the first tolling of the iron decade ahead.
